title: Cyber Defenders Unit 2 · Keys and secret codes (6-8)

items.q: Mina ranks 'maple river stone lamp' first, 'maple7' second, and 'maple' last. Why is her ranking right?
choices: A number at the end always beats extra words
Four random words are long, so a computer has far more guesses to make
A familiar single word is hardest to guess
Short passphrases are safer because they are easier to remember
items.why: Length wins. Four random words give a guessing computer far more combinations than a short familiar word.

items.q: One service has a breach and its passphrase list is copied. Why is reuse the real danger?
choices: The leaked service will close every account at once
Nothing changes, because stolen lists are never shared
The list can be traded and tried on other accounts, so one leak opens them all
A breach only matters if you lose your device
items.why: A reused passphrase turns one leak into many. The stolen list gets tried everywhere you used it.

items.q: A locked server room door and a firewall: how should they be classified?
choices: The door is physical security and the firewall is digital security
Both are digital security, because both use computers
The door is digital security and the firewall is physical security
Both are physical security, because both block entry
items.why: One guards a place you can touch, the other guards data. Physical versus digital is about what is being protected.

items.q: Sam proves it is him with a fingerprint, then a clerk checks the list to see if the parcel is his. What are the two checks, in order?
choices: Authorization, then authentication
Encryption, then authorization
Authentication, then authorization
Both checks are authentication
items.why: First prove who you are (authentication), then check what you may open (authorization). The order matters.

items.q: Why does a code sent to your phone protect you better than a second passphrase?
choices: Phone codes are longer than any passphrase
It adds a second passphrase that is easier to remember
It is faster, so attackers give up sooner
It is a different kind of check: something you have, not just something you know
items.why: Two checks of the same kind can fall together. A phone code is something you have, a different kind from something you know.

items.q: Why can a fake page not steal a passkey the way it can steal a passphrase?
choices: Fake pages are blocked on every device
Your device keeps the key and proves it is you, so there is no copyable secret to hand over
Passkeys are longer, so no page can copy them
A passkey is hidden inside a picture
items.why: A passkey never leaves your device as a typeable secret, so a fake page has nothing to copy.

items.q: Why is brute force a real threat to a shift cipher but not to a modern cipher?
choices: Shift ciphers use letters and modern ciphers use numbers
Trying keys only works when a trusted adult allows it
A shift cipher has only 25 keys to try, while a real key space is far too large to try in time
Modern ciphers have no keys, so there is nothing to try
items.why: Trying every key is quick when there are only 25. A modern key space is too large to finish in time.

items.q: A note is hidden inside a picture but the words are unchanged. What is true?
choices: That is hiding, not scrambling: anyone who finds it can read it
That is encryption, because the picture acts as a key
That is decryption, because the words are plain
That is brute force, because finding it takes time
items.why: Hiding keeps the words plain for anyone who finds them. Scrambling is what changes the words themselves.

items.q: A message uses end-to-end encryption. What can the service carrying it read?
choices: Everything, because it delivers the message
Only the sender name, but all of the words
The plain words, if the receiver agrees later
None of the plain message: only the sender and receiver can read it
items.why: End-to-end means the middle cannot read it. Only the two ends hold the keys.
